readerTitle: Why the closest-looking move is often the farthest
caseNote: 가상 사례 (원예 매장, 사무실 청소 회사, 치과 예약 소프트웨어) · 수치 없음
insight: 성장 아이디어의 거리는 상품이 얼마나 비슷해 보이는지가 아니라 고객, 역량, 판매 경로 중 몇 가지가 바뀌는지로 잰다.
misconception: 지금 파는 것과 비슷한 상품이면 가까운 확장이고 안전하다.

sources.text: Zook, C. with Allen, J. (2001). Profit from the Core. Harvard Business School Press.
Zook, C. (2004). Beyond the Core. Harvard Business School Press.

factChecks.note: 4번 카드의 Zook(Bain & Company) 책 언급은 책의 일반적 주장(강한 핵심 사업에서 너무 멀리 나간 성장 시도가 자주 실패한다)만 적었습니다. 구체적 성공률 수치는 의도적으로 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 책 제목, 연도, 저자 표기를 확인하세요.
원예 매장, 청소 회사, 치과 소프트웨어 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 3번 카드의 '바뀌는 것 개수'는 설명용 단순화이며 실제 분석에서는 각 변화의 크기도 다릅니다(7번 카드에서 언급).

cards.title: Why the closest-looking move is often the farthest
body: A garden center and an office cleaning company both want to grow. Each picks a new line that looks almost identical to what it already sells.
Both moves turn out to be far harder than expected. The reason is the same, and it has little to do with the product.

image.label: Two small businesses each looking at a signpost with two paths
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 원예 매장, 오른쪽에 사무실 청소 밴. 각각 앞에 갈림길 표지판이 있고, 가까워 보이는 길은 안개 속으로 길게 이어지고, 멀어 보이는 길은 짧고 밝다. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The garden center's next line
body: You run a busy garden center. Homeowners come on weekends to buy plants, soil and tools for their yards. You have space for one new line. Which is the safest step?

options.text: Cut flowers and bouquets. It's plants, and we know plants
options.feedback: The product looks familiar, but the buyers, timing and skills are new. You gain a natural-sounding story and take on several unknowns at once.

options.text: Outdoor furniture and grills for the same yard customers
options.feedback: It looks unrelated, but the same people buy it on the same weekend trip for the same yard project. Only the supplier is new.

options.text: A landscaping crew that designs and plants whole yards
options.feedback: Same customers, so demand is easier to find. But you'd be running crews, quotes and schedules, a different business inside your store.

cards.title: Measure distance by what changes.
body: Bouquets look closest but change the most. Gift buyers shop on weekdays, flowers spoil in days, and arranging is a skill your staff don't have.

breakdown.label: Outdoor furniture
breakdown.detail: New supplier. Same customers, store, staff and weekend rhythm.

breakdown.label: Landscaping crew
breakdown.detail: Same customers. New skills and a new way of working.

breakdown.label: Cut flowers
breakdown.detail: New buyers, new daily rhythm, new skill.

cards.title: Core and adjacent moves
body: Your **core** is the customers you serve best, the things you do best, and the way you reach those customers.
An **adjacent move** changes one of these and keeps the rest. Each thing you keep is an advantage you carry in. Each thing that changes is something you must learn from scratch.
Chris Zook of Bain & Company argued in *Profit from the Core* (2001) that many failed growth attempts came from moving too far from a strong core, too fast.

image.label: Rings around a core: customers, capabilities, channels
image.brief: 동심원 인포그래픽. 가운데 "Core", 그 주변에 "Customers", "Capabilities", "Channels" 세 조각. 바깥 링에 작은 화살표 하나만 한 조각을 넘어가는 모습 "Adjacent: change one". 더 바깥에 세 조각을 모두 넘는 화살표 "Far: change all".

cards.title: The cleaning company's trap
body: The cleaning company serves office managers on yearly contracts, working at night. Home cleaning looks like the obvious next step: same mops, same skills.
But it means new customers, small one-off jobs, daytime visits and marketing to households. Almost nothing carries over except the mops.
A closer step: restocking kitchens and restrooms for the offices it already cleans. Same buyer, same contract, same night visit.

image.label: Night office cleaning crew restocking a break room
image.brief: 밤의 사무실 탕비실. 청소 직원이 바닥을 닦는 동시에 커피, 종이컵, 휴지를 채워 넣는 장면. 같은 방문 한 번에 두 서비스가 이뤄진다는 느낌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Each step becomes your new core.
body: Adjacent moves win because they reuse what you've already paid for: customer trust, staff know-how, delivery routes, a sales relationship.
They also compound. Once furniture works, the garden center knows bulky deliveries. Now a shed or patio line is one step away, though it was two steps away before.
**A series of short steps** can carry a business far from where it started, with less risk than one big leap.

cards.title: Close isn't always right.
body: Counting changes is a rough guide. One change can be huge: a new channel, like selling online for the first time, can be harder than three small changes.
Shared assets only matter if customers want the new thing. Selling more to the same people fails if they don't need it.
And if your core market is shrinking, staying close means shrinking with it. Then a bigger move may be the safer one.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your app handles appointment booking for dental clinics. Clinic managers love it. You want a second product. Which is the most adjacent move?

options.text: Billing and payment reminders for the same clinics
options.feedback: Same users, same sales team, same data you already hold. Only the feature is new, so you can sell it in your next renewal call.

options.text: A general project tool for any small business
options.feedback: Bigger market on paper, but new users, new product and crowded competition. Your clinic reputation counts for almost nothing there.

options.text: A marketplace selling dental supplies to your clinics
options.feedback: Same buyers, which helps. But stock, shipping and returns are skills a software team doesn't have.

cards.title: Grow by changing one thing at a time.
body: Before chasing a new line, ask: will the customers, the skills or the way we reach people change? The fewer that change, the more of your advantage you keep.
**Try it today:** write down your next growth idea. Mark each of the three as *same* or *new*. If all three are new, look for a closer step first.
